name: Jamal Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm 27, and I pick and pack at a big electronics fulfilment centre out by the ring road, mostly the late shift, two till half ten. I grab a handheld scanner, it tells me which aisle and bin, I pull phone cases, chargers, headphones, then I pack them at a bench and the boxes go down the conveyor. On a good night I'm at about 140 picks an hour, which is middle of the pack.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work and the time goes quick when you've got a rhythm. I like the lads on my aisle, especially Dev, who I eat with at the ten-minute break. What wears me out is the rate screen, that number on the wall telling you you're two percent behind, and my knees after ten hours of mezzanine stairs on peak weeks.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My girlfriend Leila, she's a dental nurse, and we rent a two-bed flat above a bakery. No kids yet. I've got about three months of bills put by, which feels decent but not exactly safe. I'm the kind of guy who tries every new app first, and I use an AI chat thing most days, for my budget, for meal plans, for questions about the forklift test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud on the group chat: told you so, it was a fancy autocomplete. At work I'd say the same thing I say now, which is the robots in aisle nine still get stuck on a dropped bag. Online I'd probably post something like, at least my rent didn't get automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it means the job stays a job. Picking is hands-on, and if AI only trims the routine stuff, maybe the scanner gets smarter routes and the rate screen goes up a bit. I'd still be on the mezzanine at nine at night lifting totes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the late shift and finish the forklift licence I've been eyeing, because it pays about a pound an hour more. I'd keep using the AI tools at home for my budget and to quiz myself for the test. And I'd keep putting £150 a month in the savings pot like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, if I'm honest. I don't need the world to change, I need a bit more money and better knees. It feels like the next few years are mine to plan, not someone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rate screen might go up. What happens if the smarter scanner pushes your target from 140 to 160?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be annoyed for a month and then I'd hit it, because that's what happens every time they change something. Dev would struggle more than me, he's got a bad wrist. I'd probably show him the short-cuts I've found through the mezzanine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Leila do with the extra pound an hour from the forklift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put it straight in the deposit fund, because we want to buy a little place in about four years. Leila keeps a spreadsheet and she's stricter than me. The forklift money would be the first thing I've earned that goes on a house, not on rent.

say: I'd say **AI was hype** and the robots in aisle nine still get stuck on dropped bags.
I'd joke online that at least my **rent** didn't get automated.
think: Picking stays a **hands-on job**, maybe with smarter scanner routes and a higher rate target.
A target rise from **140 to 160 picks** would be annoying but manageable for me.
do: Finish the **forklift licence** for about a pound an hour more.
Keep putting **£150 a month** into savings and use AI to quiz for the test.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, because his plans for the next few years feel like his own.
S0.quote: The forklift money would be the first thing I've earned that goes on a house, not on rent.
fieldNote: He treats AI as a **personal tool** at home, not a threat at work.
His concern runs to **Dev's wrist**, not himself, when targets rise.
The **house deposit** with Leila is the real goal driving every choice.

steps.text: Finish the forklift licence course at the depot this spring
Put the extra forklift pay into the house deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads it's coming for the office lot first, the people who book the trucks and answer the customer emails. On the floor I'd say keep an eye on the aisle nine robots, because once they stop getting stuck they'll multiply. Online I'd say learn the robots, don't fight them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the picking part of my job has maybe five or six years left as it is. The planners upstairs will shrink first, and then the money they save buys more of those shelf-moving robots. I'd rather be the guy who fixes them than the guy they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robot maintenance course the company already runs on Saturdays, the one hardly anyone takes. I'd ask my shift manager, Karen, to put me on the robot zone when they need cover. And I'd keep the forklift licence plan going as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but also kind of excited, which I know sounds weird. It's like watching weather come in and you've got a coat. I've got a coat, I just need to put it on in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, again, and the older guys on goods-in who've been there fifteen years and don't touch phones. My friend Dev jokes that he'll be the last human picker in the building, but he isn't really joking. I'd try to drag him onto the Saturday course with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be excited. What would you tell Leila when you came home with that news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila the warehouse is changing and I'm getting on the right side of it before it does. She'd ask how much the course costs, and I'd say nothing, the company pays. Then she'd ask why nobody else takes it, and I wouldn't have a good answer.

say: I'd say AI hits **office jobs first**, like truck booking and customer emails.
On the floor, I'd say **learn the robots**, don't fight them.
think: Picking as it is has maybe **five or six years** left.
Money saved upstairs will buy **more robots**, so I'd rather fix them than be replaced.
do: Sign up for the company's **Saturday robot course**.
Ask Karen to put him on **robot zone cover** shifts.
Keep the **forklift licence** plan as a backup.
feel: **Uneasy** about the timeline but also **excited** to get ahead of it.
S1.quote: My friend Dev jokes that he'll be the last human picker in the building, but he isn't really joking.
fieldNote: He reads the **sequence** clearly: office tasks first, then savings fund robots.
A free **company course** nobody takes is his main opening.
His worry for **older colleagues** runs deeper than worry for himself.

steps.text: Join the company's free Saturday robot maintenance course
Ask the shift manager for cover shifts in the robot zone
Keep studying for the forklift licence as a backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one's scary for everyone, not just us, because the office people get hit in two years and we get hit in five. At work I'd tell people to start learning something now while there's still a gap. Online I'd probably share every article I could find about what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my picking job is gone by 2031, maybe sooner if the company gets cheap robots early. The planning and the scheduling upstairs would go in 2028, and then nobody's left to argue for keeping people on the floor. I'd have about five years, and that's not long when you're starting from a forklift ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd do the robot course and push to get onto the maintenance team within a year, even on lower hours. I'd use AI tools every night to learn basic electrics and the software they run on. And I'd up the savings from £150 to £300 a month by cutting the takeaways and my gym membership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my stomach go tight. I'm not scared of the robots, I'm scared that the company would only need six maintenance techs and there's two hundred of us. I'd want to be one of the six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to be one of the six. What if you're not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd want to have a second skill that isn't warehouse at all. Maybe electrical installation, like solar panels on roofs, because roofs are messy and robots are bad at messy. I'd look at a night course at the college on Northgate in the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house plan in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably pause it. I wouldn't sign up for a 25-year mortgage on a job I think ends in five years. Leila's job is safer, people still need someone holding the suction tube, so maybe we'd rent longer and buy on her wage.

say: I'd say **everyone** gets hit, office staff by 2028 and warehouses by 2031.
I'd tell coworkers to **start learning** something now while there's a gap.
think: My **picking job** is probably gone by **2031**, maybe sooner.
There'd only be room for a **handful of technicians** out of two hundred pickers.
do: Push onto the **maintenance team** within a year, even on fewer hours.
Double savings to **£300 a month** by cutting takeaways and the gym.
Study **basic electrics** at night with AI tools as a second skill.
feel: A **tight stomach**, less about robots and more about the **competition** for few tech jobs.
S2.quote: I wouldn't sign up for a 25-year mortgage on a job I think ends in five years.
fieldNote: He clearly uses the **three-year gap** between AGI and robots as runway.
The **house purchase** is the first thing he'd sacrifice, not his training.
He sees **Leila's job** as the household's steadier anchor.

steps.text: Get onto the warehouse robot maintenance team within a year
Raise monthly savings to £300 by cutting takeaways and the gym
Take a night course in electrical installation at the Northgate college
Delay the house purchase and keep renting on Leila's wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same storm with a slightly longer warning, so there's no excuse not to get ready. At work I'd keep pushing people onto the Saturday course. Online I'd say five years is enough time to learn a trade if you start this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years to AGI and eight to robots feels like it might actually work out for me. That's enough to get the forklift ticket, do the robot course, and then a proper electrical qualification. I'd be about 35 when the robots get good, which isn't too late to have a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence this year and the robot course alongside it. Next year I'd start a two-year part-time electrical course, paying maybe £1,200 a year out of savings. I'd keep using AI to plan my study and test myself, like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a way I can manage. It feels like a long climb rather than a cliff. I can see the top of it, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to pay for the electrical course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday Leila and I talked about, Portugal next summer, would become a week at her mum's instead. And I'd sell my old games console and stop the streaming subscriptions we never watch. That's maybe £400 right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it's manageable. What part of that picture still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What bothers me is the guys who won't do any of it. In eight years, half my shift will be out of work at the same time, and they'll all be going for the same few jobs. I don't want to be the one who made it while my mates didn't.

say: I'd say it's the **same storm** with a longer warning, so get ready.
I'd tell people **five years** is enough to learn a trade if they start now.
think: **Eight years** until robots gives me time for a **second career**.
I'd be about **35** when robots get good, which isn't too late.
do: Get the **forklift licence** and robot course done this year.
Start a part-time **electrical course** next year at about £1,200 a year.
Swap the **Portugal holiday** for a week at Leila's mum's.
feel: **Nervous** but manageable, like a **long climb** rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: In eight years, half my shift will be out of work at the same time, and they'll all be going for the same few jobs.
fieldNote: The extra years turn panic into a **staged plan** with clear costs.
His remaining worry is **guilt** about colleagues who won't adapt.
He still expects his **picking job** to end, so the mood stays anxious.

steps.text: Get the forklift licence and finish the robot course this year
Pay about £1,200 a year for a part-time electrical course
Swap the Portugal holiday for a week at Leila's mum's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. At work I'd say the same thing I always say, get on the Saturday course. Online I'd say this is when you pick your next career, not when the robots turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years to AGI and thirteen to robots means I could ride out the warehouse for a good while. I'd be 40 by the time robots are doing the picking. That's long enough to buy the house, maybe have a kid, and change job in my own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with picking and the forklift ticket for now and go back to the house deposit plan. I'd do the robot course anyway, because it's free and I like it. In a few years I'd decide between robot maintenance and electrical work based on what's actually hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's far enough away that I can plan around it, close enough that I won't forget. I'd probably think about it every few months, not every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in about four years like we planned, with a mortgage we could cover on one wage if we had to. Leila and I would sit down and do that sum properly first. That's the one rule I'd keep from the scarier pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that you think people would get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People would get lazy, I'd bet money on it. My uncle Ray (a retired miner) always says the pit closure was announced years ahead and nobody believed it until the gates shut. I'd try not to be one of those.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift and wasting it is on you.
I'd say this is when you pick your **next career**, not later.
think: I could ride the warehouse until **about 40** before robots arrive.
There's time to **buy the house**, maybe start a family, then switch jobs.
do: Return to the **house deposit** plan for about four years from now.
Take the free **robot course** anyway and decide later what's hiring.
feel: Fairly **calm**, thinking about it **every few months** rather than every night.
S4.quote: My uncle Ray (a retired miner) always says the pit closure was announced years ahead and nobody believed it until the gates shut.
fieldNote: A decade of warning brings back the **house and family** plans he'd shelved.
He keeps one rule: a **mortgage on one wage**.
His uncle's **pit closure** story shapes his fear of complacency.

steps.text: Buy a house in about four years with a one-wage mortgage
Take the free robot course and watch which jobs are hiring
Keep picking on the late shift and finish the forklift ticket

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because five years until the robots isn't enough for two hundred people to all retrain at once. What would help is the company opening the robot course to everyone on paid time, not Saturdays, and the college running electrical courses at night that a shift worker can actually get to. Paid time is the difference between three people taking it and fifty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who should pay for all the retraining. I'm in the middle on most things, but I think if the company saves millions on robots, some of that should pay for the people they used to need. That's not a handout, that's paying back.

headlineQuote: If the company saves millions on robots, some of that should pay for the people they used to need.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old picker** on the late shift at an electronics fulfilment centre.
He's an **early adopter** who uses AI daily and sees robot maintenance as his way forward.
His plans revolve around a **house deposit** with Leila, a dental nurse.
He moves from **calm** in AI Plateau to anxious when AGI comes fast, then calm again with a decade.
He worries more for **older colleagues** like Dev than for himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because five years is too short for two hundred **pickers** to retrain at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid time** for the company's robot course, and **night courses** shift workers can reach.
